questions.title: Why does Orthogonal Finetuning preserve pairwise angles between neurons?
questions.question_body: In Section 3 the paper states that OFT applies an orthogonal matrix \(\mathbf R\) to a pretrained weight matrix so that "pairwise angles between neurons are provably preserved". I understand that an orthogonal transformation preserves inner products, but I am confused about how this translates into preserving angles between *columns* of \(\mathbf W^0\) (i.e., neurons). Does this hold for any orthogonal \(\mathbf R\) applied on the left side only? And how does this angle preservation relate to retaining semantic knowledge from pretraining?

questions.title: How does the Cayley transform guarantee orthogonality during training?
questions.question_body: The paper mentions using Cayley parameterisation \(\mathbf R=(\mathbf I+\mathbf Q)(\mathbf I-\mathbf Q)^{-1}\) where \(\mathbf Q=-\mathbf Q^\top\). I am unsure how gradient updates on \(\mathbf Q\) keep \(\mathbf R\) exactly orthogonal at every step. Could someone walk through why \((\mathbf I+\mathbf Q)(\mathbf I-\mathbf Q)^{-1}\) always yields an orthogonal matrix when \(\mathbf Q\) is skew‑symmetric, and what happens if \(\mathbf I-\mathbf Q\) becomes singular?

questions.title: What is the intuition behind modeling dense orthogonal matrix factorisation as an information‑transmission problem?
questions.question_body: Section 3 introduces a "grid‑structured graph" where each factor \(\mathbf B_i\) corresponds to directed edges between adjacent levels, interpreting non‑zero entries as possible information flows. I struggle to see how this graphical view captures the algebraic constraints of orthogonality and why dense connectivity across all levels corresponds exactly to having a dense product \(\mathbf R=\prod_i \mathbf B_i\). Could someone explain this mapping in simpler terms, perhaps with a tiny example (e.g., \(d=4,m=2$)?

questions.title: How do butterfly graphs achieve dense connectivity with only \(O(d \log d)\) edges?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that a butterfly topology can connect every source node to every destination node using only \(O(d \log d)\) non‑zero entries (edges), compared to \(O(d^2)\) for a dense matrix. I am having trouble visualising this edge count. For instance, with \(d=8") how many edges are there in each butterfly component, how many components are needed (i.e., value of \(m")), and how do those numbers add up to roughly \(8 \log_2 8 = 24")?

questions.title: Why does BOFT$(m,b)$ have exactly $\frac{1}{2}(b-1)d m$ effective trainable parameters?
questions.question_body: In Section 4 it is stated that BOFT$(m,b)$ uses $\frac{1}{2}(b-1)d m$ parameters for a layer of size $d \times n$. I understand each $2b \times 2b$ block requires $(b-1)b$ degrees of freedom when represented via a skew‑symmetric matrix, but I cannot derive the full expression accounting for all $m$ components and their block placements. Could someone provide a step‑by‑step derivation linking block size $b$, number of factors $m$, and total parameter count?

questions.title: Why can’t standard Dropout be applied directly to BOFT’s multiplicative weight update?
questions.question_body: "Multiplicative Dropout" is introduced because conventional Dropout “does not work” with BOFT’s update $\mathbf R(m,b)$. I’m unclear on what goes wrong if we simply drop entries of $\mathbf R$ after it has been computed (or drop elements of its factors). Is it because dropping would break orthogonality? How exactly does selecting whole butterfly components or diagonal blocks preserve orthogonality while still providing regularisation?

questions.title: How does block size $b$ affect the trade‑off between expressivity and parameter efficiency in BOFT?
questions.question_body: Figure 3 shows that increasing $b$ reduces parameter count but seems to worsen approximation error when trying to mimic a random dense orthogonal matrix. Conversely, smaller $b$ with larger $m$ gives better approximation with fewer parameters overall. Could someone clarify intuitively why larger blocks make the model less expressive despite having fewer components, and how one should choose $(m,b)$ for a given layer dimension $d$?

In practical terms—forward pass time per layer, backward gradient computation—how much extra cost should we expect compared with ordinary OFT’s single block‑diagonal matrix? Are there recommended implementation tricks (e.g., caching products or fusing operations)?"
